Explain how a simple rain gauge measures rainfall, why its opening and measuring tube may have different diameters, and two common sources of inaccurate readings. Use plain accurate prose. Aim for approximately 120–170 English tokens.

message.content: A simple rain gauge collects rain in a vertical cylinder with an open top. Rainfall depth is read from a measuring tube, often marked in millimetres or inches. If the opening is wider than the tube, the same rainfall volume is concentrated into a smaller area, amplifying the depth so light rain can be measured accurately. This ratio must match the gauge design. Two common errors are obstruction and evaporation. Debris, snow, or ice can block the funnel, while wind can deflect drops or blow collected water out. Water may also evaporate before reading, especially in hot weather. Splash from surrounding surfaces and an unlevel gauge add further error. For reliable data, the gauge must be level, exposed, cleaned, and read promptly.
